DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
The pilot gives Thornbury useful evidence, and the cost table adds up. But several central claims in the paper and in your description contradict its own data. The flats result is the reverse of what the text says. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce. Most importantly, the local plant can take only part of the projected tonnage. Once these are corrected, the service is unlikely to be fully covered by the £520,000 allocation.

## Major issues

**1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate to houses.**
Table 1 shows participation of **66% in houses and 21% in flats**, so houses took part at more than three times the rate. Flats households also put out less food waste each week (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg). Section 2's statement that participation was "broadly similar across housing types" is incorrect. So is the conclusion that no separate approach for flats is needed. The data actually point the other way: flats probably need a different service, such as communal food bins, different caddy arrangements or targeted engagement. That's typical of food waste schemes generally.

**2. The projection uses a 64% participation rate; the pilot achieved 57%.**
Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but Table 1 gives 57% overall. The pilot's housing mix of 20% flats also matches the district's, so 57% can be applied directly.

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| Paper (64% × 1.9 kg) | ≈ 3,290 t |
| Pilot overall rate (57% × 1.9 kg) | ≈ 2,930 t |
| By housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg; flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | ≈ **2,870 t** |

The projection overstates tonnage by about 13%, and the disposal saving by about **£30,000 a year**: roughly £212,000 rather than £243,000.

**3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes; the projection needs about 2,900–3,300.**
Section 4 says Brookfield can offer up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until 2029. That leaves roughly 1,100 tonnes on the corrected projection, or 1,500 on the paper's own figure. The paper doesn't say where that waste goes. The options are:
- **The next AD plant, 46 miles away.** The gate fee isn't stated, and there would be substantial extra haulage costs in vehicle time, fuel and crews off-round.
- **Leaving it in the residual bin.** Then the £74-a-tonne saving is lost on that portion, while the collection costs are still incurred.

If only the Brookfield tonnage earns the saving, it is about **£133,000**, not £243,000. Your description's statement that "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is true for less than two-thirds of the projected waste. Brookfield's expansion would ease this from 2029, but that's two years after launch and isn't guaranteed.

**4. The service is not shown to be fully funded.**
- Net cost with the corrected tonnage, all assumed to go to Brookfield-equivalent treatment: £733,400 − £212,000 ≈ **£521,000**. That's already at the £520,000 allocation.
- Net cost if only 1,800 tonnes earn the saving: £733,400 − £133,000 ≈ **£600,000** or more, plus haulage or gate fees for the remainder. That's a gap of at least about **£80,000 a year**.

The £520,000 is also described as "provisional," following funding the Government has "indicated." Cabinet should be told it isn't confirmed. Approval would commit the Council to about £990,000 of vehicle spending up front.

## Costs that are missing or unclear

Your description says "every cost line is shown." Several aren't:
- **The helpline and web page** in Section 6 have no line in Table 2.
- **Crew cover and on-costs.** It isn't clear whether £34,000 per operative includes employer National Insurance, pension and cover for leave and sickness, which typically adds 15–25% to staffing. Supervision, recruitment and training are also absent.
- **Capital financing.** Vehicle costs are depreciated over seven years, but borrowing costs on £990,000, and the up-front cost of caddies for 52,000 households, aren't shown.
- **Ongoing liners.** Households get a three-month supply. Whether the Council keeps supplying liners after that, and at what cost, needs stating.
- **A spare vehicle.** Six vehicles for six rounds leaves no cover for breakdowns or servicing.
- **Haulage to a second plant,** as described in point 3.

## Smaller issues

- **Statutory timing.** Under the Simpler Recycling reforms, English councils were generally required to introduce weekly household food waste collections by 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils with existing contracts. A start date of April 2027 needs a clear explanation of Thornbury's position. If no transitional arrangement applies, the paper should say so and address the compliance risk.
- **Vehicle lead time.** Ordering in December for delivery in March assumes a three-month lead time. Lead times for specialist refuse vehicles are often much longer. The timetable should be confirmed with the supplier, and a fallback such as hired vehicles should be identified.
- **Pilot duration and novelty.** Six months, from January to June, may capture early enthusiasm. Participation often drops after launch, and food waste varies seasonally. The projection should allow for some fall-off.
- **The satisfaction survey.** The 81% is from "surveyed pilot households." If most respondents were participants, it overstates satisfaction across all households. The response rate and how it compares with the 57% participation should be reported.
- **Rounding in Table 1.** The overall figure per participating household is about 1.86 kg, shown as 1.9. That's fine, but it slightly overstates tonnage if used unrounded.

## What holds up

- The participation rates within Table 1 are correct: 66%, 21% and 57%.
- The cost arithmetic is right: vehicles at £141,400, crews at £408,000, a total of £733,400, and a net cost of £490,400 on the paper's assumptions.
- The £74-a-tonne saving and the paper's £243,000 figure are correctly calculated from its own inputs.
- Low contamination (under 2%) and falling missed-collection reports are genuinely encouraging.
- The overall structure and implementation sequence are sensible.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct Section 2 to report the gap between houses and flats, and set out a specific approach for flats.
2. Rebase the projection on 57%, or better, on participation by housing type (about 2,870 tonnes).
3. Show where the tonnage beyond 1,800 goes, with gate fees and haulage costs for the second plant.
4. Add the missing costs: helpline, on-costs and cover, spare vehicle, liners and financing.
5. Present the net cost as a range against the provisional funding, and identify how any gap would be met.
6. Clarify the statutory position and confirm vehicle lead times.

In short, the pilot supports introducing the service, but not the claims that it can be uniform across housing types, treated locally or fully funded. Cabinet should see the corrected figures, likely a net cost of roughly £520,000–£600,000 or more against a provisional £520,000, before authorising the £990,000 vehicle order.
